gnarled.e:
First attested Shakespeare 1603:
: Thy sharpe and sulpherous bolt Splits the vn-wedgable [unwedgable] and gnarled Oke [oak].
: Measure for Measure, Act II, scene ii, line 116
Variant of knurled, from knurl. By surface analysis, gnarl + -ed, though gnarl is a later back-formation. Popular use by 19th century.

s.d: used of old persons or old trees; covered with knobs or knots
x: gnarled and knotted hands
a knobbed stick

s.d: Knotty and misshapen.
Made rough by age or hard work.

gnarly.e: From gnarl (“knot in wood”) + -y. The slang senses were particularly popularized by US surf culture in the 1970s.

s.d: used of old persons or old trees; covered with knobs or knots
x: gnarled and knotted hands
a knobbed stick

s.d: Having or characterized by gnarls; gnarled.
x: a gnarly stump
Out of one window I can see the garden, those mysterious deep-shaded arbors, the riotous old-fashioned flowers, and bushes and gnarly trees.

s.d: (dated, slang) Excellent; attractive.
x: a gnarly dude
There ain't nothing gnarlier (apparently) than slapping on some brightly coloured sunblock to ward off the blinding spectre of dangerous, snow-reflected sunlight.

s.d: (US, dated, slang) Dangerous; difficult.
x: a gnarly problem
When the swell struck, the North Shore got gnarly, and the wise ones hit the outer islands where the energy was just as juicy but a bit more organized.

s.d: (US, slang) Unpleasant, awful, ugly.
x: We're not talking about a lame chick and a gnarly guy. We're talking about a couple of far-out dudes.
Funky Kong: 'Those Snowmads are a gnarly bunch! I hear they're enjoyin' your island. Go get 'em, DK!'

gnash.e: From Middle English gnasten. Origin unknown; the word is probably either Germanic or ultimately onomatopoeic. Compare Old Norse gnastan, Danish gnaske ("munch", "crunch"), German knirschen, German Low German gnirschen, gnörschen (“gnash”), Swedish gnissla (“squeak; gnash”), all of onomatopoeic origin.

s.d: A sudden snapping of the teeth.
grind together, of teeth
To grind (one's teeth) in pain or in anger.
x: gnashing your teeth

s.d: (figuratively) To clash together violently.
x: There they were, boiling up in snowy spouts of spray, smiting and gnashing together like the gleaming teeth of hell.

s.d: To run away.

gnat.e: From Middle English gnat, from Old English gnætt (“gnat; midge; mosquito”), from Proto-West Germanic *gnatt, *gnattu, from Proto-Germanic *gnattaz, *gnattuz (“gnat”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰneHdʰn-, *gʰneHd- (“to gnaw; scratch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰen- (“to gnaw; bite; scratch; grind”). Cognate with Low German Gnatte (“gnat”), dialectal Swedish gnatt (“mosquito”), German Gnatz (“scabs; rash; scabies; stinginess”). Related also gnit and gnaw.

s.d: any of various small biting flies: midges; biting midges; black flies; sand flies
(British usage) mosquito
A biting insect, especially a mosquito.
x: [A]nd his servant was beside him with a fan to keep away the flies and gnats.

s.d: (informal) An annoying person.
x: "Away thou whining gnat, and trouble me not!"

s.d: (historical) A type of jet fighter aircraft.
very small North American and South American warblers
A member of any of various species of small passerine birds in the family Polioptilidae found in North America and South America, close relatives of the wrens.
x: Perhaps you'll witness a California gnatcatcher dining on gnats (of course!) or a cactus wren singing on a prickly pear pad.

s.d: the most inferior point of the mandible in the midline
A craniometric point, being the lowest part of the middle line of the mandible.
One of a set of three paired appendages on the thorax of a decapod crustacean, located just posterior to the maxillae and used in feeding.
x: An appendage which is modified to assist in feeding is known as a maxilliped or gnathopod.

s.d: A maxilliped.
a vertebrate animal possessing true jaws
Any vertebrate with jaws, including amphibians, reptiles, mammals, and most modern fish, in contrast with the Agnatha
x: Current conceptions of gnathostome phylogeny depict a rather simplistic arrangement of nominally monophyletic and, apparently, morphologically disparate groups.

gnaw.e:
From Middle English gnawen, gnaȝen, from Old English gnagan, from Proto-West Germanic *gnagan, from Proto-Germanic *gnaganą (“to gnaw”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *gʰnēgʰ- (“to gnaw, scratch”).
Cognate with Dutch knagen, German nagen, Danish gnave (“to gnaw”), Norwegian Bokmål gnage, Norwegian Nynorsk gnaga, Swedish gnaga.

s.d: The act of gnawing.
x: give something a gnaw
have a gnaw of a bone

s.d: bite or chew on with the teeth
x: gnaw an old cracker

s.d: To bite something persistently, especially something tough.
x: The dog gnawed the bone until it broke in two.
Ten thousand men that fishes gnaw'd upon

s.d: To produce excessive anxiety or worry.
x: Her comment gnawed at me all day and I couldn't think about anything else.

s.d: To corrode; to fret away; to waste.

gneiss.e: From German Gneis, from Middle High German gneist (“spark”), from Old High German gneisto (“spark”). More at gnast.

s.d: a laminated metamorphic rock similar to granite
(uncountable) A common and widely-distributed metamorphic rock having bands or veins, but not schistose.
x: The old towns along the route are as solidly built from the gneiss of the region as you might expect.

s.d: small tropical tree with tiered branches and divaricate branchlets having broad glossy dark green leaves; exploited for its edible young leaves and seeds that provide a fine flour

gnocchi.e: From Italian gnocchi, plural of gnocco (“dumpling”, literally “lump”), related to nocchio (“knot (in wood)”), a borrowing from Lombardic knohha (“knuckle, bone, knot”), from Proto-Germanic *knukô (“bone”), *kneukaz (“tuber, knuckle”), from Proto-Indo-European *gnew- (“knot, bundle”). Cognate with Middle High German knoche (“bone, knot”) (modern German Knochen), Middle Dutch knoke (“knuckle, knob, knot”), Swedish knoge (“knuckle”). More at knuckle.

s.d: (Italian) a small dumpling made of potato or flour or semolina that is boiled or baked and is usually served with a sauce or with grated cheese
(uncountable) Italian pasta-like dumpling(s) made of potato or semolina.
x: Test one gnocchi by placing it in a large pot of rapidly boiling lightly salted water.

Silky, feather-light and with an other-worldly texture, home-made gnocchi is one of the most spoiling things you can make for someone, yet it is surprisingly simple to put together, especially when just for two.

gnome.e: From French gnome (“gnome”), from New Latin gnomus, used by Paracelsus as a synonym for pygmaeus (“pygmy”).

s.d: a legendary creature resembling a tiny old man; lives in the depths of the earth and guards buried treasure
a short pithy saying expressing a general truth
An elemental (spirit or corporeal creature associated with a classical element) associated with earth.
x: He adopts the Rosycrusian fancy of Gnomes, spirits which inhabit the earth, and who by their power form the ores of metals, and all the wonders met with in the inmost recesses of the globe.

s.d: One of a race of imaginary human-like beings, usually depicted as short and typically bearded males, who inhabit the inner parts of the earth and act as guardians of mines, mineral treasure, etc.; in modern fantasy literature and games, when distinguished from dwarves, gnomes are usually smaller than dwarves and more focused on engineering than mining.
x: When the trees were disposed of, the gnomes vanished again.

There were not one but four gnomes standing at his feet. “I nearly trod on you,” Daniel said. “What are you doing here?”
The gnomes just stood, looking up at him.

s.d: (derogatory, informal) A person of a small stature or misshapen features, or of a strange appearance.
The mountain pygmy owl, Glaucidium gnoma, a small owl of the western United States.
A small statue of a dwarf-like character, often bearded, placed in a garden.
x: There were ornamental ponds and shrubs clipped into animal shapes, painted concrete gnomes sitting on mushrooms, pink flamingos standing on one leg[.]

s.d: An upper atmospheric optical phenomenon associated with thunderstorms, a compact blue starter.
(derogatory) A banker, especially a secretive international one.

So far the major beneficiaries of the boom in gold have been deposed South American dictators, Middle Eastern potentates, and the gnomes of Zurich.

s.d: A brief reflection or maxim; a pithy saying.

gnomic.e: From French gnomique, ultimately from Ancient Greek γνωμικός (gnōmikós), from γνώμη (gnṓmē, “thought, judgement”), akin to γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “know”). By surface analysis, gnome + -ic.

s.d: Mysterious and often incomprehensible yet seemingly wise.

gnomon.e:
Borrowed from French gnomon, or directly from its etymon Latin gnōmōn, or directly from its etymon Ancient Greek γνώμων (gnṓmōn, “discerner, interpreter; carpenter’s square; gnomon of a sundial; (geometry) gnomon”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to be aware of; to perceive; to know”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”); the word is thus related to know.
The geometry sense (sense 4) is from the resemblance of the plane figure to a carpenter’s square. Similarly, a gnomon in mathem

s.d: indicator provided by the stationary arm whose shadow indicates the time on the sundial
An object such as a pillar or a rod that is used to tell time by the shadow it casts when the sun shines on it, especially the pointer on a sundial.
x: [T]he gnomon being the upright, and the shadow the side, the square-root of the sum of the squares is the hypotenuse; […]

s.d: An object such as a pillar used by an observer to calculate the meridian altitude of the sun (that is, the altitude of the sun when it reaches the observer's meridian), for the purpose of determining the observer's latitude.
The index of the hour circle of a globe.
x: Index of a globe, the little style or gnomon, which being fixed on the pole of the globe, and turning round with it, points out the hours upon the hour circle.

s.d: A plane figure formed by removing a parallelogram from a corner of a larger parallelogram.
x: If a Parallelogram be divided into four leſſer ones, by two Lines interſecting each other; and one of theſe Parallelograms be retrench'd, or taken away; the other three will make a Gnomon, ordinarily call'd a Square.

s.d: A number representing the increment between two figurate numbers (“numbers equal to the numbers of dots in geometric figures formed of dots”).

s.d: intuitive knowledge of spiritual truths; said to have been possessed by ancient Gnostics
(uncountable) An immanent form of knowledge or transcendent insight, such as sought by the Gnostics.

gnostic.e: From Ancient Greek γνωστικός (gnōstikós, “relating to knowledge or knowing”), from the root of verb γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to come to know, to learn”) + -τῐκός (-tĭkós) or from γνῶσις (gnôsis, “knowledge, knowing”) + -κός (-kós, adjective suffix), depending upon the analysis.

possessing intellectual or esoteric knowledge of spiritual things
